passages.title: EU AI Act: the four risk tiers
passages.text: The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) sorts an AI system into one of four tiers: Prohibited (Article 5 practices banned outright, e.g. social scoring or untargeted facial scraping), High-Risk (Annex III categories such as employment, credit scoring, or law enforcement, which require conformity assessment and ongoing risk management), Limited Risk (Article 50 transparency duties, e.g. telling users they're talking to a chatbot), and Minimal Risk (no specific obligations under the Act).
passages.source: Case 01 -- AI Act Risk Navigator, risk_engine.py taxonomy

passages.title: EU AI Act Article 5: prohibited practices
passages.text: Article 5 bans specific practices outright regardless of context: subliminal or manipulative techniques that cause significant harm, exploiting vulnerable groups, social scoring, individual crime-risk profiling based solely on profiling, untargeted scraping of facial images to build a database, emotion recognition at work or in school, inferring sensitive traits from biometric data, and real-time remote biometric identification in public by law enforcement outside three narrow exceptions.
passages.source: Case 01 -- AI Act Risk Navigator, Article 5 taxonomy

passages.title: EU AI Act Annex III: high-risk categories
passages.text: Annex III lists eight sectors where an AI system is presumed high-risk: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services (credit, insurance, benefits), law enforcement, migration/asylum/border control, and the administration of justice or democratic processes. A narrow procedural-task exception under Article 6(3) can take a system out of this tier, but that exception must be actively assessed and documented, never assumed.
passages.source: Case 01 -- AI Act Risk Navigator, Annex III taxonomy

passages.title: EU AI Act Article 50: transparency obligations
passages.text: Article 50 requires that people be told when they are interacting with an AI system (unless obvious from context), that AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content be machine-readably labelled as synthetic, and that emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation systems disclose their operation to the people exposed to them.
passages.source: Case 01 -- AI Act Risk Navigator, Article 50 taxonomy

passages.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework: the four functions
passages.text: NIST's AI RMF organises AI risk management into four functions: Govern (establish policies, roles and accountability for managing AI risk across the organisation), Map (identify the context and risks of a specific AI system before and during development), Measure (assess, benchmark and monitor those risks with appropriate metrics), and Manage (prioritise and act on risks, including response and recovery).
passages.source: NIST AI RMF 1.0, referenced in Case 01's cross-mapping

passages.title: What a Model Card is for
passages.text: A Model Card documents a model's intended use, out-of-scope uses, training and evaluation data, performance metrics, and known limitations, so anyone deciding whether to rely on the model has the information to do so responsibly rather than treating it as a black box.
passages.source: Case 03 -- Governance Documentation Suite, model_card.md.j2; Mitchell et al. (2019)

passages.title: How the risk assessment's overall risk level is computed
passages.text: This program scores overall risk as probability (Low/Medium/High) crossed with severity (Low/Medium/High) through a simple lookup table, producing Low, Medium, High, or Critical. The matrix is deliberately simple so a reviewer can sanity-check the result by hand in ten seconds rather than trusting an opaque score.

passages.title: Human oversight models: in/over/out-of-the-loop
passages.text: Human oversight design distinguishes three models: in-the-loop (a human approves every decision before it takes effect), over-the-loop (a human monitors and can intervene, but decisions execute automatically by default), and out-of-the-loop (the system acts fully autonomously with no real-time human check). The higher the system's risk tier, the stronger the oversight model it should carry, and the escalation and contestability paths should be documented regardless of which model is chosen.

passages.title: Data governance basics for an AI system
passages.text: A system's data governance statement should record where its training and input data comes from, whether it contains personal data (PII), and what governance measures apply -- minimisation, retention limits, access controls, and anonymisation where relevant -- so data handling can be reviewed independently of the model itself.

passages.title: Why third-party AI vendors get a separate questionnaire
passages.text: When an AI system is sourced from a vendor rather than built in-house, the vendor's own data handling, security posture, and support for audits and evidence requests become part of the system's risk picture. A Vendor AI Risk Questionnaire captures those answers even for internally-built systems, so the same evidence set applies uniformly across the AI inventory.

passages.title: Why every AI system needs an incident response runbook
passages.text: An incident response runbook defines severity levels, who gets notified, and what containment action to take when an AI system misbehaves in production -- a biased outcome, a safety failure, a data leak -- so the response doesn't have to be improvised under pressure.

passages.title: How to register a new AI use case
passages.text: To register a new AI use case, describe what the system does, who it affects, and what data it uses. This assistant will classify its risk tier using the same rule-based approach as the AI Act Risk Navigator, and file an intake request through its one allowlisted tool. A Prohibited or High-Risk system is queued for a governance reviewer's approval before the intake is marked submitted; a Limited or Minimal risk system is auto-approved and logged immediately.
passages.source: Case 05 -- Governed RAG/Agent, this project's own intake workflow
